thread_b.role: file final put cleanup (lockless fast-path reader)

emergent_bug.violated_requirement: ρ = atomic([read(file->f_ep)]) from thread_b (the lockless __fput fast-path read of the pointer must not interleave with a conflicting write)
emergent_bug.missing_guarantee: thread_a clears f_ep while holding the epoll lock, but eventpoll_release()'s fast-path check reads f_ep deliberately OUTSIDE the epoll semaphore (to avoid acquiring it); a one-sided lock does not serialize the lockless read → no g establishes atomic(read)
emergent_bug.category_rationale: ρ is atomic over a single pointer read; an unmarked lockless load concurrent with a conflicting store → data race

fix_maps_to: WRITE_ONCE() on the f_ep stores in __ep_remove/attach_epitem and READ_ONCE() on the eventpoll_release fast-path read → marks the accesses as single-copy-atomic (establishes atomic(read/write) at the C-memory-model level); the intentional racy fast path is preserved, only annotated
recall_risk_notes: Clean one-sided-lock pointer race; unprotected reader yields atomic(read) directly. Risks: (1) the race is EXPLICITLY intentional/benign by design (commit: 'annotate racy check'; eventpoll_release re-validates under the semaphore on the slow path and the file has no other referrers), so an LLM may judge the fast-path read a sufficient/benign guard and reject the report — exactly the §4.6.9 guard-sufficiency judgment that can cut either way. (2) Object identity: thread_b reaches file->f_ep via __fput -> eventpoll_release(file) while thread_a reaches it via epi->ffd.file; static aliasing must prove these are the same struct file to ground same_location.
